If there is no profile preference yet, then browser language is a reasonable fallback. I’d keep it in English for system administrators or shared service accounts if that is the standard operational language, but otherwise the user’s saved preference should win.

context_question: For the rollout across the university and faculties, what training or onboarding should each role receive so they can start using the system effectively, and are there any roles that need a different level of support or timing than the standard onboarding?
answer: University and faculty administrators would need the most structured training, especially on approvals, delegation, thresholds, and reporting, because they are making policy-level decisions in the system. Department staff would need practical hands-on onboarding focused on updating inventory, handling requests, and releasing or reserving items, while ordinary requestors mostly need a short guided introduction on how to search, submit requests, and track status. I’d give super users or local champions extra training before go-live so they can support others, and I’d probably stagger rollout for departments that manage more complex assets or have heavier booking activity.

context_question: Which department characteristics should trigger a staggered rollout, and are there any thresholds or exceptions for when a department should be included in an early phase versus waiting for a later one?
answer: Departments that have lots of assets, frequent reservations, or more complicated approval chains should probably go later, because they need more preparation and testing. Early phase departments would be the simpler ones, with fewer item types and fewer cross-department dependencies, so we can validate the workflow without too much risk. If a department is already using fairly clean data or has a local champion ready to help, that could be an exception and make them suitable for an earlier rollout.

context_question: What specific criteria or thresholds should determine that a department is simple enough for an early rollout, and what would make you keep an otherwise simple department until a later phase?
answer: A department would be early-rollout ready if its inventory is relatively small, its requests are mostly straightforward, and it does not rely heavily on shared rooms or cross-faculty approvals. I’d hold it back if the data is messy, if staff are still unsure about their existing processes, or if they depend on a lot of manual exceptions that the new system would have to replicate. Even a simple department should wait if its local champion is unavailable or if they are in the middle of a busy period like exams or lab setup.

context_question: What practical signs or thresholds would tell you that a department is too messy or too dependent on manual exceptions to be considered ready for the early rollout?
answer: If the inventory records are incomplete, duplicated, or not updated in a long time, that would be a clear sign it is too messy for early rollout. The same goes for departments that handle a lot of special-case approvals outside the normal process, or where staff cannot agree on who owns which assets or who approves what. If they would need a lot of cleanup just to get the system usable, I’d keep them for a later phase.

context_question: When you’re keeping those shared definitions up to date over time, who should be able to propose changes, who should approve them, and how should changes be communicated so departments stay aligned?
answer: Proposals should be allowed from university-level admins and also faculty admins, since they are the ones closest to the operational changes. Approval should sit with the university inventory owner or a central governance group, because we need one source of truth across all three faculties. Once a change is approved, it should be announced through the system itself and also by email to the affected departments so nobody is working from an outdated definition.

context_question: When should a department be allowed to proceed with rollout despite a local champion being unavailable or the department being in a busy period, if ever?
answer: If the department is truly low-risk, with a small inventory and very simple workflows, we could still proceed without the local champion for a short delay, but only if another trained person can cover day-to-day questions. A busy period is trickier; I’d only go ahead if the work is urgent and we can reduce the scope, because otherwise adoption usually suffers. In most cases I would rather wait than force a rollout when the team is overstretched.

context_question: When an approved change affects only some departments or needs to take effect urgently, what should determine who gets notified and whether the notice goes out immediately or on a scheduled basis?
answer: The affected departments should be determined by which faculty, department, or asset category the change actually touches, so only people who rely on that definition get the notice. If it is urgent, like a policy or approval change that could cause mistakes right away, the notice should go out immediately. If it is routine or planned, it can be scheduled for the next business day or a maintenance window so departments are not interrupted unnecessarily.

context_question: For request statuses, are there any special rules for which statuses are allowed to be changed, reused, or mapped across faculties so that everyone uses the same meaning consistently?
answer: Yes, there should be a standard set of request statuses across all faculties, and only the central inventory team should be able to change that definition. Faculties should not invent their own meanings for the same status, because that would confuse reporting and approvals. If a faculty needs a local variation, it should be mapped back to the standard status set rather than creating a new one.

context_question: When you refer to shared assets, what naming rules should govern items like equipment, rooms, and software licences so that the same asset type is named consistently across faculties and clearly distinguishes shared from faculty-owned items?
answer: We should have one agreed naming convention for each asset type, with a standard label, a location or owner code, and a unique identifier so people can tell similar items apart. Shared assets should be clearly marked as university-owned or shared, while faculty-owned items should carry the faculty code in the name or tag. I would avoid letting each faculty make up its own wording, because that makes search and reporting much harder.

context_question: How should the naming convention handle assets that move between faculties or change ownership over time so the tag remains consistent and searchable?
answer: The unique identifier should stay the same even if the asset moves, and only the ownership or location fields should be updated. That way the tag remains searchable in history and we do not lose track of where it came from. If ownership changes permanently, we should record the old owner as part of the audit trail rather than renaming the asset from scratch.

context_question: When a request status has a local faculty-specific variation, what are the rules for mapping it back to the standard status set in reports and exports, especially if the local status does not match any standard status exactly?
answer: The local status should always map to the closest standard status that has the same business meaning in reports and exports. If there is no exact match, then it should be flagged for review and not silently forced into a misleading standard status. I’d want the central team to approve any new mapping so the same local status is interpreted the same way everywhere.

context_question: For approved changes, should the notice go only to the specific departments, faculty, or asset categories directly affected, and are there any legal, policy, or technical exceptions that would require a broader audience or a different delivery timing?
answer: Yes, the default should be to notify only the directly affected departments, faculties, or asset categories. We would broaden it only if there is a university-wide policy impact, a legal requirement, or a technical dependency that could affect other users or systems. In those cases the timing might also need to change, especially if waiting would create compliance or operational risk.
